title: Day60 for Chrome on LinkedIn
text:
Our Chrome extension still follows one rule: it never reads LinkedIn pages.

What's new is that it's now useful on LinkedIn anyway.

On a LinkedIn job, press "Find it with Day60". It looks for the same opening on the company's own careers page. If the company doesn't post it there, you paste the description.

On a LinkedIn profile, a second button saves that person to one of your jobs as the hiring manager, their boss, an internal champion or the recruiter.

How, without reading the page? It uses only the tab's address and title, and only when you press its button. It never fills in forms, never applies and never sends a message. You send every message.

That's slower than a tool that does everything for you. It's also the only way I'd want someone reaching out in my name.

Free in the Chrome Web Store. Link in the first comment.

title: Three touches, then stop
text:
Day 0, day 2, day 7. Then stop.

It's easy to send one message and give up, or to send ten and get muted. Three touches is the middle ground: a first note about their problem, a two-line nudge with something new, and a kind last word.

Day60 caps it at 3 touches per person and tells you when each follow-up is due. You send every one.

Save this for your next follow-up. Link in bio to try one job free.

title: Would Tick let you send it
text:
Would Tick let you send it?

We ran one cold email through Day60's free message checker.

The first draft: 7 things to fix. It opened with "I". The subject line ran 12 words. There was no clear question, two em dashes, and the phrases "I wanted to reach out" and "passionate".

The rewrite: one line about their team, one line of proof, one clear question. All 13 rules pass.

Pick what you're sending (a cold email, a LinkedIn connection note, or the message after they accept), paste your draft, and Tick tells you what to fix and why.

Tick checks the rules, not the facts. Make sure every detail is true.

Free, no sign-up: getday60.com/message-checker

title: What Day60 is and isn't
text:
Most job tools make applying faster.

I built one that slows you down to the few jobs worth your time, then gets you to the person who decides.

What it is:
A 60-day job-search sprint. Up to 3 new jobs a day.
For each job, the four people closest to the hire: the hiring manager, their boss, an internal champion and the recruiter. Verified work emails where available.
A short draft in your voice, checked against writing rules before you send it.

What it isn't:
An auto-apply bot. It never applies and never sends.
A LinkedIn hack. It never logs in to LinkedIn, scrapes it or automates it.
A blast tool. No mass messages, no keyword stuffing.

Keep your tracker and your résumé tool. Day60 is the part after you find the job.

Try it on one job. Link in the first comment.

text:

title: Four people who decide
text:
If someone you care about has sent out application after application and heard nothing, this one's for them.

Every job has four people who decide who gets hired: the hiring manager, their boss, someone on the team who knows the work, and the recruiter. An application usually reaches only one of them.

A short note to the hiring manager, about their team and ending with one clear question, puts your name in front of the person who decides. The slides show what to send each of the four.

title: Most job searches are single-threaded
text:
Most job searches are single-threaded.

In sales, a deal with only one contact is called single-threaded. Everyone in sales knows how those go. One person gets busy, and the whole deal goes quiet.

A job search usually runs the same way. One application, one recruiter, one inbox. If that recruiter is buried this week, so are you.

Every job has four people who shape the hire:
The hiring manager, who feels the empty seat.
Their boss, who approved the role.
Someone on the team who knows what the job really needs.
The recruiter, who runs the process.

You don't have to write to all four on day one. But know who they are, and make sure the hiring manager hears from you directly, in a short note about their team.

That's the method I built Day60 around: one job, four people, a few well-researched messages, and you send every one.
